sec.title: Background
sec.p: Acute lung injury (ALI) can initiate early epithelial remodeling that may precede pulmonary fibrosis, with EMT of alveolar epithelial cells implicated in this acute phase. While mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-derived exosomes exhibit repair potential, their conventional culture conditions fail to mimic the hypoxic microenvironment of ALI. Here, we explored the therapeutic effects and regulatory mechanisms of hypoxia-preconditioned bone marrow MSC-derived exosomes (HExos) in LPS-induced ALI with early epithelial remodeling.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: BMSCs were characterized via osteogenic/adipogenic differentiation and flow cytometry. Exosomes derived under normoxia (NExos) and hypoxia (HExos) were isolated and validated using nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Western blot. An LPS-induced ALI mouse model was employed to evaluate exosome efficacy. Through integrated miRNA sequencing, luciferase reporter assays, and gain-/loss-of-function experiments, we examined a working model involving the miR-486a-5p/Skp2/GATA4 axis.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: HExos markedly alleviated LPS-induced acute lung injury and early-stage collagen deposition. Mechanistically, HExos were enriched with miR-486a-5p, which directly targeted Skp2, thereby reducing Skp2-mediated ubiquitin–proteasome degradation of GATA4 and attenuating EMT-like changes. Notably, miR-486a-5p mimics reversed EMT-like changes in alveolar epithelial cells, while its knockdown abolished the protective effect.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Hypoxia-preconditioned bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cell (BMSC) exosomes demonstrate significant potential to alleviate LPS-induced acute injury and early epithelial remodeling by engaging a miR-486a-5p/Skp2/GATA4 working model, offering a proof-of-concept therapeutic strategy for ALI.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Acute Lung Injury (ALI) and its severe form, Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), are devastating clinical conditions with high morbidity and mortality rates [1–3]. Pathologically, they involve diffuse alveolar damage, excessive pulmonary inflammation, and alveolar epithelial cell (AEC) apoptosis [4]. Persistent or recurrent injury may disrupt repair mechanisms, potentially leading to irreversible pulmonary fibrosis—a major clinical challenge due to its poor reversibility, adverse impact on patient prognosis, and significant quality-of-life burden [5]. Thus, developing novel therapies to halt fibrosis progression holds critical clinical value.

Recent studies highlight the pivotal role of alveolar epithelial cell epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in pulmonary fibrosis progression [6]. Deciphering EMT’s molecular mechanisms could revolutionize therapeutic strategies for ALI-associated fibrosis. Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) have emerged as promising candidates for lung disease treatment [7], demonstrating exceptional efficacy against ALI and fibrosis [8, 9]. Current evidence indicates MSC therapy primarily functions through paracrine signaling [10], where secreted growth factors, anti-inflammatory mediators, and bioactive compounds multi-targetedly ameliorate ALI pathology: enhancing epithelial repair, reducing vascular leakage, improving alveolar clearance, and regulating immune responses [9, 11].

Exosomes, the principal paracrine effectors of MSCs, are nanosized vesicles (50–150 nm) formed through multivesicular body-plasma membrane fusion, featuring a distinctive bilayer membrane structure [12, 13]. These natural carriers efficiently deliver bioactive cargo (proteins, mRNAs, miRNAs) and mediate critical intercellular communication [14]. Compared with whole-cell transplantation, exosome therapy retains comparable therapeutic effects while offering superior advantages including minimal immunogenicity and enhanced safety [15]. Notably, MSC-derived exosomes exert antifibrotic effects via specific miRNA mechanisms: miR-21a-5p attenuates renal fibrosis by targeting PFKM [16], while miR-192-5p suppresses scar fibrosis via the IL-17RA/Smad axis [17]—providing robust molecular evidence for exosome-based interventions.

The oxygen microenvironment critically regulates MSC functionality [18, 19]with conventional normoxic culture conditions failing to recapitulate physiological oxygen levels [20]. Hypoxic preconditioning potently enhances MSC proliferation, migration, viability, and therapeutic efficacy [21, 22]. While hypoxia-primed MSCs demonstrate superior anti-fibrotic effects in renal fibrosis models compared to normoxic counterparts [21], their exosomal functions in pulmonary fibrosis remain elusive. We hypothesize that hypoxic preconditioning may amplify exosomal anti-fibrotic effects through cargo optimization.

As pivotal exosomal effectors, miRNAs play central roles in ALI and fibrosis regulation [23–25]. Notably, miR-486a-5p and related miRNAs constitute 43–59% of BMSC exosomal content [26], with miR-486a-5p specifically attenuating pulmonary fibrosis via TGF-β1 pathway inhibition [27].Mechanistically, the ubiquitin-proteasome system—particularly the SCF-Skp2 complex—modulates fibrotic progression [28–30]. Skp2 deficiency alleviates renal fibrosis [31], and its inhibitors show therapeutic promise for pulmonary fibrosis [32]. Our bioinformatics analysis identifies transcription factor GATA4 as a novel Skp2 substrate, with GATA4 implicated in multi-organ fibrosis [33, 34], suggesting the miR-486a-5p/Skp2/GATA4 axis as a potential regulatory cascade.

This study evaluated hypoxia‑preconditioned bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes in LPS‑associated acute lung injury with epithelial remodeling, focusing on: (1) attenuation of injury and early epithelial remodeling, and (2) whether exosomal miR‑486a‑5p constrains EMT‑like changes via the Skp2–GATA4 pathway. These findings may inform strategies to modulate ALI‑associated remodeling.

sec.title: Cell culture and hypoxia treatment
sec.p: BMSCs were isolated and expanded using established protocols. Passages 3–5 were cultured in OriCell™ medium supplemented with exosome-depleted FBS (Cyagen, Guangzhou) under either: Normoxia (21% O₂, 5% CO₂, 37 °C) or Hypoxia (1% O₂, 5% CO₂, 37 °C) for 48 h. MLE-12 alveolar epithelial cells (iCell Bioscience, Shanghai) were maintained in Starfish Biotechnology-specified medium supplemented with 10% exosome-depleted FBS (Cyagen, Guangzhou) under normoxic conditions (21% O₂, 5% CO₂, 37 °C).

Hypoxic preconditioning was performed in a Forma 3131 water-jacketed incubator at 1% O₂, 5% CO₂, and 37 °C. The O₂ sensor (± 0.1% accuracy) was calibrated using the manufacturer-recommended air-span method (20.7% O₂) before each experiment. O₂ stability at 1% was verified over 48 h via manual recordings at 0, 6, 12, 24, 36, and 48 h (1.0 ± 0.2%, Fig. S1A).

All post-hypoxia manipulations (medium change, exosome collection, cell lysis, CCK-8 assay) were performed in a custom 1% O₂ workstation (Shanghai Yuyan S1007 controller + acrylic glove box B01) via vacuum-transfer chamber (≤ 60 s air exposure, O₂ fluctuation < 0.3%; Supplementary Fig. S1B).

sec.title: Characterisation of mouse MSCs
sec.p: To characterize mouse BMSCs, adipogenic and osteogenic differentiation were induced as previously described [35, 36]. Cells at the third passage were used for differentiation assays.
For adipogenesis, cells at 100% confluence were cultured in adipogenic medium (Cyagen, China) replaced every 3 days. After 21 days, cells were fixed with 4% PFA and stained with Oil Red O.
For osteogenesis, cells at 70–80% confluence were cultured in osteogenic medium (Cyagen, China) replaced every 3 days. After 21 days, cells were fixed with 4% PFA and stained with Alizarin Red S.
Surface markers (CD90, CD44, CD71, CD29, CD45, CD34; BioLegend) were analyzed by FACS (BD Accuri C6 Plus) and FlowJo.

sec.title: Exosome isolation and characterization
sec.p: When bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells (BMSCs) reached 80–90% confluence, the culture medium was replaced with exosome-depleted fetal bovine serum (FBS) (10%), and conditioned medium was collected every 48 h. Exosome purification involved sequential centrifugation: 300 × g for 10 min (cell removal), 2,000 × g for 15 min (debris clearance), and 10,000 × g for 30 min (large particle elimination). The supernatant was filtered (0.22 μm) and ultracentrifuged (100,000 × g, 1 h, 4 °C; Sorvall Lynx 6000, Thermo Scientific, USA). The pellet was washed with PBS, re-ultracentrifuged under the same conditions, and resuspended in PBS for downstream assays.

Exosome characterization included: Size distribution via nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA; Flow NanoAnalyzer U30E, NanoFCM, China); Surface marker detection (CD81, CD63, TSG101, CD9) by Western blot (Zen-Biosciences, China); Morphological analysis using transmission electron microscopy (TEM; Tecnai G2, FEI, USA); Protein quantification via BCA assay (Beyotime Biotechnology, China).

For cellular uptake assays, exosomes were labeled with Dil dye (ExoPDil10-1 Kit, Rengen Biosciences, China):4 mg/mL Dil was incubated with exosomes, purified via column, and co-cultured with MLE-12 mouse alveolar epithelial cells, Cells were fixed (4% PFA, 30 min) and imaged by fluorescence microscopy (Nikon, Japan).

sec.title: Flow cytometry apoptosis assay
sec.p: Cells were labeled using the YF®488-Annexin V/PI Apoptosis Kit (Cat. #Y6002, Luelandy, China) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Apoptosis was analyzed via flow cytometry (BD Accuri C6 Plus, BD Biosciences, USA) using Annexin V/PI dual staining. Briefly, transfected MLE-12/LPS cells were harvested, resuspended in 1× binding buffer, and incubated with Annexin V and PI for 15 min in the dark. Apoptotic cells were then quantified by flow cytometry.

sec.title: Cell culture and model establishmen
sec.p: MLE-12 cells were seeded into 6-well plates. Upon reaching 70–80% confluence, they were stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 500 ng/mL) for 24 h. Subsequently, 40 µg of Exos or HExos was added to each well, with PBS serving as the control.

sec.title: Mouse model of LPS-Induced acute lung injury with early remodeling and treatment
sec.p: Eight-week-old C57BL/6 mice were acclimatized for 1 week under standard conditions. The ALI model with early epithelial remodeling was established by daily intraperitoneal injection of LPS (5 mg/kg; Sigma, USA) for 5 consecutive days [37–40]. Mice were randomly divided into four groups (n = 10/group): control (saline), LPS, Exos + LPS, and HExos + LPS. On day 1 post-LPS, Exos + LPS and HExos + LPS groups received tail vein injections of Exos or HExos (100 µL, 1 µg/µL), repeated weekly for 3 doses. In a parallel experiment, mice were similarly divided into control, LPS, LPS+NCKDHExos, and LPS+miRKDHExos groups (n = 10/group) with identical protocols. All mice were sacrificed on day 21 post-LPS for lung collection. All procedures strictly followed the guidelines of the Fujian Provincial Hospital Experimental Animal Welfare and Ethics Committee to minimize suffering.

sec.title: HE staining, immunohistochemistry, and masson staining
sec.p: The left lung tissue of each mouse was fixed in 10% formalin for at least 48 h, then dehydrated with acetone and embedded in paraffin. Section (4 μm thick) were stained with hematoxylin-eosin (H&E), while immunohistochemical staining was performed using the Masson trichrome kit (Solarbio, China) to assess collagen deposition. For immunohistochemistry, an immunohistochemical kit (Maxim, China, #KIT-9707) was used. Sections were blocked with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 30 min at 4 °C, followed by overnight incubation with primary antibodies: TGF-β (Proteintech, USA, #21898-1-AP), E-cadherin (Zenbio, China, #340341), Vimentin (Zenbio, #R22775), α-SMA (Proteintech, #67735-1-Ig), and Skp2 (Zenbio, #R382104). Subsequently, biotinylated secondary antibodies (Maxim, #KIT-9707) were applied for 1 h at 37 °C. Sections were observed under an optical microscope (Nikon, Japan).

sec.title: Hydroxyproline assay
sec.p: Lung tissue collagen concentration was determined using the kit (ZCi bio, China, #ZC-S0383) protocol: Tissue samples were hydrolyzed in lysis buffer at 100 °C for 2–6 h. Absorbance of the resulting chromogen was measured at 560 nm, and hydroxyproline content was calculated as µg/mg wet weight.

sec.title: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
sec.p: Exosomes were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PBS), loaded onto a copper mesh (ciamite, China, #BZ11022b), and incubated in the dark. After PBS washes, exosomes on the mesh were stained with 50 µL of 1% phosphotungstic acid (2 min), air-dried, and imaged using TEM (Tecnai G2, FEI, USA). structure.

sec.title: MiRNA sequencing analysis
sec.p: Comparative miRNA expression profiles of normoxic BMSC-derived exosomes (BMSCs-Exos) versus hypoxia-treated BMSC-derived exosomes (BMSCs-HExos) were analyzed at Hunan Nojiu Biotechnology Co., Ltd (Changsha, China), with three biological replicates per group. RNA was extracted using the miRcute miRNA Isolation Kit (Tiangen, China, #DP501), and RNA quantity/quality assessed via Nanodrop One (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Libraries were prepared using the QIAseq miRNA Library Kit (Qiagen, Germany, #331505), then quantified by Qubit® 2.0 fluorometer (Life Technologies, USA) and size-verified via Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, USA). Sequencing was conducted on Illumina HiSeq X Ten (Illumina, USA), with library construction and sequencing services provided by Shanghai New Group Group. miRNA expression levels (counts) were quantified by aligning reads to miRBase for known miRNAs and novel miRNA prediction. Differentially expressed miRNAs were identified using CPM (counts per million) normalization and DESeq2 analysis, retaining those with |log2FC| > 1 and p < 0.05 for downstream analysis.

sec.title: Protein Immunoblotting
sec.p: Proteins were extracted using RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime Biotechnology, China) and quantified via BCA assay (Beyotime Biotechnology, China). For each sample, 40 µg protein was resolved on 10–15% SDS-PAGE gels and transferred to PVDF membranes. After blocking with 5% BSA (1 h, RT), membranes were incubated overnight (4 °C) with primary antibodies (1:1000): TGF-β (Proteintech, USA, #21898-1-AP), E-cadherin (Zenbio, China, #340341), Vimentin (Zenbio, #R22775), α-SMA (Proteintech, #67735-1-Ig), TSG101 (Zenbio, #R25999), CD9 (Zenbio, #R380441), SNAIL (Zenbio, #340942), Skp2(Zenbio,# R382104),CD63 (Zenbio, #R23327), CD81 (Zenbio, #R381296), GATA4 (Zenbio, #R381799), HIF-1α (Zenbio, #340462),β-actin (Zenbio, #R23613), and GAPDH (Zenbio, #R24404). Membranes were then incubated with secondary antibody (1:5000, 37 °C, 1 h). Signals were detected using ECL Kit (Uelandy, China) and analyzed with Image Lab software.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence staining
sec.p: Cells in 12-well plates were fixed with 4% PFA (20 min), PBS-washed, then permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 (20 min, RT). After blocking with 3% BSA (30 min), cells were incubated with primary antibodies (1:100, 4 °C, overnight): E-cadherin (Zenbio, China, #340341) and Vimentin (Zenbio, #R22775). Following PBS washes, fluorescent secondary antibody was applied (1 h, RT). Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI and visualized using a fluorescence microscope (Nikon, Japan).

sec.title: Quantitative RT-PCR
sec.p: Total RNA was isolated using TRIzol® (Invitrogen, USA). For mRNA, cDNA was synthesized with PrimeScript RT reagent (Takara, Japan) and qPCR performed using SYBR Premix Ex Taq (Takara) on QuantStudio 5 (Thermo Fisher, USA). miRNA analysis employed miRcute kits (Tiangen, China; #DP501 for isolation, #KR211 for cDNA) with LightCycler® 96 (Roche) using SYBR Green Master Mix (#FP411). Data were normalized to GAPDH/U6 (2-ΔΔCt method). Targets included: miR-486a-5p, miR-210-3p, miR-101a-3p, miR-486a-3p, miR-101c, miR-145b, miR-455-3p, miR-503-5p, miR-20a-5p, miR-21a-3p, U6, Skp2, Vimentin, TGF-β, α-SMA, E-cadherin, and GAPDH. Primers (Shangya Biotech, China) are detailed in Additional file 1: Table S1.

sec.title: Luciferase reporter assay
sec.p: The predicted miR-486a-5p binding sequence in Skp2 3’-UTR was PCR-amplified and cloned into psicheck2.0 to generate psicheck2.0-Skp2-wt. A mutant vector (psicheck2.0-Skp2-mut) was similarly constructed. HEK293T cells (1 × 10^5/well) in 24-well plates were co-transfected using Lipofectamine 3000 (GlpBio, USA) with miR-486a-5p mimics/control mimics and wild-type/mutant vectors. Empty psicheck2.0 vector co-transfection served as control. Luciferase activity was normalized to empty vector+control mimic group.

sec.title: Lentiviral transduction
sec.p: LV2-mmu-miR-486a-5p-inhibitor (miRKD) and control LV2 (miR-NCKD) vectors were constructed (Shengzhe, China). BMSCs (40–50% confluent) were infected at optimal MOI. miR-486-5p mimic/NC mimic were synthesized (Banma Biotech, China). pcDNA3.0-Skp2 was generated by cloning Skp2 cDNA (Abm, China), while Skp2 shRNA (Abm) was used for knockdown. LPS-treated MLE-12 cells (1 × 10^6/well in 6-well plates) at 80–90% confluence were transfected with specified plasmids using Lipo3000 (GlpBio) for 48 h before harvesting.

sec.title: Cycloheximide (CHX)-based protein stability and ubiquitination assays
sec.p: MLE-12 cells were treated with 20 µg/ml CHX (Sigma, USA) for various durations, then lysed for immunoblotting. Protein levels were quantified using ECL Kit (Uelandy, China) and Image Lab software. For ubiquitination assays, cells transfected with miR-486a-5p mimic, inhibitor, or OE-Skp2 plasmid were immunoprecipitated with specific antibodies followed by IB analysis.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data represent mean ± SEM (n = 3). GraphPad Prism 9 was used for all analyses: unpaired t-tests (two-group comparisons) and one-way ANOVA (multi-group comparisons). Significance was set at p < 0.05 (*P < 0.05; **P < 0.01).

sec.title: Identification of Bone Marrow Mesenchymal Stromal cells (BMSCs)
sec.p: BMSCs were isolated from mouse bone marrow using density gradient centrifugation, with passages 3–5 used for characterization. Morphologically, 80–90% confluent cells exhibited a typical spindle shape (Fig. 1A). Multilineage differentiation potential was confirmed by: Osteogenic differentiation (Alizarin Red-positive) and Adipogenic differentiation (Oil Red O-positive) (Fig. 1B). Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated positive expression of CD29, CD44, CD90, and CD71, but negative for CD34 and CD45 (Fig. 1C).

sec.title: Identification of MSC-derived exosomes
sec.p: To assess oxygen concentration-dependent effects, exosomes were isolated from BMSCs cultured under normoxic (21% O₂) or hypoxic (1% O₂) conditions for 48 h. CCK-8 showed hypoxia up to 48 h did not affect MSC viability (Fig. S2B)0.48 h, 1% O₂ stabilized HIF-1α (Fig. S3), confirming BMSC hypoxia.Comprehensive characterization included: Physicochemical properties: NTA revealed a particle size of 50–150 nm (mean: 66.2 ± 23.3 nm) (Fig. 2A). TEM displayed typical cup-shaped morphology, with no intergroup differences (Fig. 2B); Marker expression: Western blot confirmed exosomal markers (TSG101, CD9, CD81, CD63) (Fig. 2C); Cellular uptake: Dil labeling demonstrated significantly higher uptake in MLE-12 cells under hypoxia vs. normoxia (Fig. 2D).

sec.title: HExos mitigate LPS-induced EMT like changes in alveolar epithelial cells in vitro
sec.p: To evaluate HExos’ regulatory role in EMT, MLE-12 cells were stimulated with 500 ng/mL LPS for 24 h to establish an EMT model. This concentration (500 ng/mL, 24 h) effectively induces EMT-related transcriptional changes in MLE-12 cells(Fig. S2A).RT-PCR and Western blot revealed that LPS downregulated epithelial marker E-cadherin and upregulated mesenchymal markers (vimentin, TGF-β, α-SMA) (Fig. 3A–C). LPS-treated cells were then exposed to PBS, Exos, or HExos for 24 h. Notably, HExos more effectively reversed LPS-induced EMT-like changes than Exos/PBS, restoring E-cadherin and suppressing vimentin, TGF-β, and α-SMA.Immunofluorescence further confirmed the expression changes of E-cadherin and vimentin (Fig. 3D, E).

Data are presented as the mean ± SD. from three independent experiments, * p < 0.05

sec.title: HExos mitigate LPS-induced injury and early epithelial remodeling
sec.p: To evaluate HExos’ therapeutic potential, we established a murine model of LPS-induced ALI with early epithelial remodeling (5 mg/kg, i.p. for 5 days). Experimental groups (Fig. 4A): NS control、LPS、LPS+Exos (normoxic exosomes)、LPS+HExos (hypoxic exosomes).Exosome treatment (100 µg, i.v.) began post-LPS modeling (weekly×3). No significant weight differences were observed (Fig. 4B). H&E and Masson staining show LPS‑induced alveolar injury with focal collagen deposition, both mitigated by Exos and more prominently by HExos.(Fig. 4C, D); IHC demonstrates decreased epithelial E‑cadherin and increased α‑SMA, TGF‑β, and vimentin after LPS, changes that are reversed by HExos, consistent with attenuation of EMT‑like remodeling.(Fig. 4F), quantitative analysis is presented in Supplementary Fig. S4;Hydroxyproline levels in the HExos group were significantly lower compared to those in the LPS/Exos groups (Fig. 4E).

sec.title: HExos mitigate LPS-induced EMT-like changes in alveolar epithelial cells via miR-486a-5p delivery
sec.p: Exosomal miRNAs are key mediators of intercellular communication. RNA sequencing revealed 38 upregulated and 130 downregulated miRNAs (≥ 2-fold, P < 0.05) in HExos vs. normoxic Exos (Fig. 5A, C). qRT-PCR validated 7 upregulated miRNAs (e.g., miR-486a-5p, miR-210a-3p) (Fig. 5B).Focusing on miR-486a-5p (most pronounced increase in HExos), we observed elevated expression in LPS+HExos-treated groups vs. LPS/LPS+Exos (Fig. 5D, E). Functional assays demonstrated that miR-486a-5p mimics: Reduced LPS-induced apoptosis in MLE-12 cells.Upregulated E-cadherin and downregulated vimentin/α-SMA/TGF-β (Fig. 5G, H), indicating reversal of EMT-like changes, quantitative immunoblot analysis is shown in Supplementary Fig. S5.

Data are presented as the mean ± SD. from three independent experiments, * p < 0.05

sec.title: HExos mitigate LPS-induced EMT-like changes and lung injury via miR-486a-5p delivery
sec.p: To elucidate miR-486a-5p’s role, we generated miR-486a-5p-knockdown (miRKD) BMSCs and negative controls (miR-NCKD), confirming transfection efficiency by qRT-PCR (Fig. 6A). Exosomes (miRKD-HExos/miR-NCKD-HExos) were isolated from these cells, with qRT-PCR verifying reduced miR-486a-5p in miRKD-HExos (Fig. 6B).In vitro, miRKD-HExos failed to restore E-cadherin or suppress vimentin/α-SMA/TGF-β vs. miR-NCKD-HExos (Fig. 6C, D). In vivo, miRKD-HExos-treated mice exhibited worse lung fibrosis (Ashcroft scores, collagen deposition) than miR-NCKD-HExos group (Fig. 6E, F).

sec.title: Exosome miR-486a-5p regulates ALI-associated remodeling by targeting Skp2
sec.p: To elucidate the molecular mechanism by which exosomal miR-486a-5p regulates EMT-like changes in MLE-12 cells, we employed the miRWalk 3.0 database to predict its potential target genes and prioritized Skp2, previously implicated in lung fibrosis [24]. Through dual luciferase reporter assays, we confirmed that miR-486a-5p directly binds to the 3‘-UTR of Skp2: the miR-486a-5p mimic markedly suppressed luciferase activity of the wild-type Skp2 3’-UTR versus the control, with no effect on the mutant (Fig. 7A).In the animal model, immunohistochemistry revealed that Skp2 expression was elevated in the LPS-treated group but attenuated by HExos (Fig. 7B). Consistently, in vitro experiments demonstrated that HExos reversed LPS-induced Skp2 upregulation in MLE-12 cells (Fig. 7C and D).To define Skp2’s role in EMT-like changes, we generated a Skp2 overexpression vector (pcDNA3.0-Skp2). Overexpression downregulated E-cadherin and GATA4 and upregulated mesenchymal markers (Vimentin, TGF-β, α-SMA), counteracting HExos’antifibrotic effect (Fig. 7E and F). Conversely, Skp2 knockdown ameliorated the LPS-induced EMT-like changes. (Fig. 7G).Mechanistically, miR-486a-5p mimic reduced Skp2 and elevated GATA4, while miRKDHExos yielded the opposite trend (Fig. 7H and I). Notably, Skp2 modulates GATA4 via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway: CHX tracking indicated faster GATA4 degradation with miR-486a-5p inhibitor (Fig. 7J); MG132 rescued this degradation (Fig. 7L); and co-IP verified enhanced GATA4 ubiquitination by miR-486a-5p inhibitor or Skp2 overexpression (Fig. 7M and N).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive interstitial lung disease marked by aberrant epithelial repair and matrix deposition, often leading to respiratory failure. Current antifibrotic treatments slow decline but rarely reverse disease, highlighting the need to target early remodeling. In a mouse model of LPS-associated acute lung injury with early remodeling, hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stromal cell–derived exosomes were associated with reduced injury and remodeling. Our findings support a preliminary working model in which exosomal miR-486a-5p constrains Skp2 and preserves GATA4 abundance to limit EMT-like changes, suggesting a potential avenue for exosome-based modulation of epithelial remodeling.

Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs), as multipotent stromal cells, hold immense potential in regenerative medicine [41]. However, clinical deployment faces formidable barriers: cryopreservation hurdles, functional heterogeneity, alloimmune responses, oncogenic potential, and ethical controversies. Notably, MSC-derived exosomes (MSC-Exos) serve as bioactive nanovesicles that faithfully transmit parental cell signals, thereby harnessing MSC-like therapeutic benefits while evading cell-based therapy risks [42].

Physiological oxygen tension (1–14% O₂) is markedly lower than standard in vitro culture conditions (21% O₂). Intriguingly, hypoxic preconditioning has been demonstrated to enhance MSC therapeutic potency [43] by augmenting their paracrine activity. Supporting this concept, MSC-derived exosomes were recently shown to mitigate radiation-induced lung injury [44], prompting our hypothesis that hypoxia-preconditioned exosomes (HExo) would exhibit superior therapeutic efficacy to normoxic exosomes (Exo) in acute lung injury (ALI).

Experimental validation revealed that while HExo and Exo shared comparable physical characteristics (NTA assay), HExo demonstrated enhanced cellular uptake efficiency in lung epithelial cells (MLE-12). In LPS-induced EMT models, HExo potently reversed the characteristic downregulation of the epithelial marker E-cadherin and aberrant upregulation of the mesenchymal marker vimentin [45]. Consistently, in vivo studies established that HExo not only attenuated alveolar inflammation and pathological collagen deposition but also preserved lung histoarchitecture.

Emerging mechanistic evidence has shown that MSC exosomes exert their therapeutic effects primarily through miRNA delivery. For instance, miR-142 confers radioprotection in intestinal injury [46], miR-125b-5p enhances renal tubular repair [47], and miR-125a-5p attenuates myocardial injury by modulating macrophage polarization and angiogenesis [48]. These findings collectively provide potential explanations for the enhanced efficacy of HExo.Nevertheless, the miRNA cargo profile of mouse bone marrow MSC-derived HExos and its functional impact on EMT-like changes in MLE-12 cells remain unexplored.

Our small RNA sequencing revealed that miR-486a-5p was remarkably enriched in HExos relative to Exos and was effectively internalized by MLE-12 cells, suggesting its pivotal role in mediating the superior bioactivity of HExos. Functional validation demonstrated that miR-486a-5p mimics suppressed EMT-like changes progression in alveolar epithelial cells, whereas knockdown of miR-486a-5p in BMSCs-HExos substantially compromised its EMT-inhibitory effects. These data establish that exosomal transfer of miR-486a-5p to injured MLE-12 cells constitutes the core mechanism underlying BMSCs-HExos’ protective action.

To delineate the downstream pathway, we employed bioinformatics prediction followed by experimental verification, identifying Skp2 as a bona fide target of miR-486a-5p via dual-luciferase reporter assays. Notably, Skp2, an F-box protein component of the SCF ubiquitin ligase complex, is ubiquitously expressed across tissues (heart, kidney, liver, etc.) and orchestrates diverse processes including cell cycle progression and fibrosis by governing the turnover of key substrates (e.g., p27, FOXO1) [28, 49]. Relevant to our findings, Skp2 has been implicated in TGF-β1-induced EMT and E-cadherin ubiquitination [50]. Further investigation revealed that Skp2 may target GATA4, a transcription factor linked to cellular senescence and fibrogenesis, for ubiquitin-mediated degradation.

To mechanistically validate this axis, we demonstrated through loss-and gain-of-function studies that Skp2 silencing alleviated LPS-induced alveolar epithelial injury, whereas Skp2 overexpression abolished the protective effects of HExos. Critically, ubiquitination assays unequivocally established Skp2-mediated proteasomal degradation of GATA4. Collectively, these findings support a working model in which HExos deliver miR-486-5p to downregulate Skp2, preserving GATA4 abundance and attenuating EMT-like remodeling.

While our LPS-induced model effectively captures early epithelial remodeling and EMT-like changes, it remains an acute injury paradigm and does not fully replicate the chronic characteristics of established pulmonary fibrosis, such as persistent collagen deposition, fibroblast foci, or progressive architectural distortion. Therefore, our findings should be interpreted as evidence for modulating early remodeling processes rather than indicative of a definitive anti-fibrotic effect. We fully acknowledge that the intraperitoneal LPS model is not a standard model for studying pulmonary fibrosis or its transition; rather, it is a widely used acute-lung-injury model that may initiate early remodeling events. Our study focuses on these early changes, not on chronic fibrosis. To better understand the therapeutic implications of the miR-486a-5p–Skp2–GATA4 axis, future studies should validate this pathway in standard fibrosis models, such as bleomycin or FITC-induced pulmonary fibrosis, to assess its relevance in chronic pulmonary diseases.

While this study elucidates the novel miR-486a-5p/Skp2/GATA4 axis underlying hypoxic MSC-exosome-mediated EMT inhibition in MLE-12 cells, several limitations merit consideration. First, as outlined above, the LPS model captures acute injury and early remodeling but not chronic fibrosis; hence, extrapolation to long-term fibrotic diseases should be cautious. Second, while our data suggest an association between Skp2 and GATA4, definitive evidence that GATA4 is a direct substrate of Skp2 is lacking; further validation through interaction mapping and F-box dependency analyses is needed. Additionally, although we did not track biodistribution, hUC-MSC-derived exosomes are reported to rapidly accumulate in the lung after i.v. injection [51, 52], supporting that the observed protection primarily occurs in the pulmonary compartment. Additionally, the timing and dosage of exosome administration were not evaluated, which could significantly influence therapeutic outcomes. Importantly, Klinger et al. [53]showed MSC-exosomes remain efficacious for up to 3 weeks after cessation; our study already demonstrates maintained protection at 1 week post-treatment, but durability beyond 2–3 weeks remains to be formally tested. Finally, the characterization of exosomes did not include negative markers or particle-normalized dosing as recommended by the latest MISEV guidelines, which may affect the comprehensive understanding of exosomal characteristics and efficacy. Despite these limitations, our findings contribute to the proof-of-concept that hypoxia-conditioned exosomes can effectively deliver miRNA cargo to modulate epithelial remodeling in ALI, warranting further validation in classical fibrosis models.

sec.title: Clinical translation
sec.p: We propose initiating hypoxic MSC-exosome therapy within 24–48 h of ALI/ARDS diagnosis (Berlin exudative phase, ICU days 1–3) using three weekly i.v. injections (21 days). Efficacy data stem from metabolic and nephropathy models [54, 55], while mechanistic support comes from hypoxic BMSC-exosomes delivering circ-LRP6 to preserve alveolar barrier function in LPS-ALI mice [56]. A recent COVID-19 ARDS RCT showed that 5 × 10¹⁰ hUCMSC-exosomes given ≤ 72 h safely lowered TNF-α/CRP and restored T-cell subsets [57], supplying human proof-of-concept for both early time-window and feasible dose. Multicentre, larger-scale trials across heterogeneous at-risk populations are now warranted to validate broad clinical utility.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our work identifies miR-486a-5p as a regulator of early epithelial plasticity in acute LPS-induced lung injury, acting via Skp2 repression and GATA4 stabilization (Fig. 8).These findings provide proof-of-concept that hypoxic MSC-derived exosomes can limit acute-phase EMT-like changes and transient matrix deposition, but do not establish efficacy against chronic pulmonary fibrosis. Validation in progressive fibrosis models and human samples is warranted.
